opus-5.5.text:
I'd say it happened gradually, but there were a few clear inflection points.

For a long time, robotics was mostly a control and planning field. You modeled the dynamics carefully, you wrote down the kinematics, you designed controllers, and you used optimization or search to plan motions. Learning was there, of course. People did learning from demonstration and reinforcement learning on robots back in the 2000s, but it was kind of a niche. The mainstream view was that if you understood the physics well enough, you could engineer the behavior.

The first big shift came around 2012 to 2015, after deep learning took off in computer vision. Perception was the obvious entry point. Suddenly object detection and segmentation actually worked, and roboticists who had been hand-engineering features just switched over. That part was almost uncontroversial, because the gains were so obvious.

The more interesting shift was when people started learning the *control* part, not just perception. Around 2015 to 2016 there was work on end-to-end visuomotor policies, where you go from camera pixels directly to motor torques, and the large-scale grasping experiments with many robot arms collecting data in parallel. That made people take seriously the idea that behavior itself could be learned rather than designed. Deep RL was also very hot at that time because of the results in games, and a lot of people tried to bring that to robots.

But honestly, around 2017 to 2020, a lot of that was still in the "promising but painful" stage. Real-world RL was sample-inefficient, sim-to-real had gaps, and many people in the traditional robotics community were skeptical, sometimes for good reasons. You'd see a beautiful learned demo, and then a well-tuned classical system would beat it on reliability.

I think the moment it became truly mainstream, where it became the default assumption rather than one camp, was more like 2022 to 2023. A few things came together. Large language models and vision-language models showed how much you can get from scale and pretraining. Imitation learning got much better, with things like diffusion-based policies and transformer policies trained on teleoperated demonstrations. Cheaper hardware and better teleoperation setups made it practical for a small lab to collect useful data. And then people started building larger multi-robot, multi-task datasets and talking about robot foundation models. After that, students entering the field mostly assumed learning would be at the core, and the question became how to get the data and how to make it generalize.

So if I had to give one answer: learning entered through perception in the mid-2010s, but it became the mainstream paradigm for robot behavior only in the last few years. Even now, I don't think classical methods went away. The best systems usually combine both, using learning where the world is messy and hard to model, and structure where you actually know the physics.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sim-to-real gaps and the limits of learned demos, but does not convey Kay Ke’s advisor’s judgment that simulator-only results were insufficient to establish robotics research’s value.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say it happened in stages rather than all at once. Around 2016 to 2018, deep learning had already taken over computer vision, and people in robotics started asking why it couldn't do the same for control. Deep reinforcement learning results, like the work coming out of Berkeley and DeepMind, got a lot of attention, and Google's arm farm for grasping was a signal that learning from large amounts of robot data was a serious path.

But at that point I'd still call it a strong minority. Most labs were doing model-based control, motion planning, classical perception pipelines. Learning was a promising add-on, not the center.

The real shift, in my view, came after large language models showed what scaling could do. Once people saw that pretraining on internet-scale data produced general capabilities, the question became whether the same recipe could work for embodiment. Projects like RT-1 and RT-2, the open cross-embodiment datasets, and the whole wave of vision-language-action models made learning-based approaches the default assumption for young researchers. By 2023 or 2024, if you walked into a robotics conference, the majority of papers had learning somewhere in the pipeline.

So I'd put the mainstream moment around 2023. The foundation was laid earlier, but that's when the center of gravity moved. And honestly, the field is still working out how much of the classical toolkit should survive. I don't think the answer is zero.

astra-6.text: I’d say it was a gradual shift, but if I had to pick a period, I’d point to the mid-2010s. Machine learning was already part of robotics before that, but deep learning’s success in computer vision made it much more central, especially for perception. Learning then became increasingly prominent in manipulation and control as well. So I wouldn’t name one particular year—it became mainstream at different times in different parts of robotics.

sol-6.1.text: I’d say it was a gradual shift, but around the early to mid-2010s, machine learning started becoming a mainstream direction in robotics. Before that, people were already using learning methods, but often for individual components, like perception. As deep learning became more effective, researchers began exploring whether robots could also learn manipulation and control. So I wouldn’t point to one particular year—it was more a change in how people approached the problem.
